The disease was discovered in 1954 by a pediatrician. Later, they determined that the condition was an inborn error involving branched-chain amino acid metabolism
While you might remember learning about the burnt sugar or maple syrup smell in urine, this disease can also cause that distinctive smell in earwax and sweat.
This regulatory protein was first discovered by Setsuro Ebashi in 1963 while he was investigating how calcium controls muscle contraction and relaxation
It is actually a group of proteins that consists of three subunits. These are named C (which binds calcium), I (which inhibits contraction), and T (which anchors the complex).

The name comes from the Greek word tropos, meaning 'turn' or 'change', because it helps trigger the turning/contraction of muscle fibers by shifting position when bound to calcium. We mostly measure I and T since they have cardiac-specific variants.
This was first discovered in 1947 in a forest of Uganda during yellow fever research on rhesus macaque monkeys with human infections confirmed in Uganda and Tanzania in 1952.

For many decades, this viral infection only caused sporadic, mild illnesses in Africa and Asia. The virus arrived in Brazil in 2015 and spread rapidly across South and Central America and doctors noticed a sudden, alarming spike in babies born with microcephaly.
This led to the WHO declaring this a Public Health Emergency of International Concern as researchers proved the virus could pass from pregnant individuals to fetuses

The earliest evidence of infections caused by this organism in humans came from an archeological site in Brazil where four human fossilized stool samples from 7850 to 5280 BCE tested positive by ELISA

The first person to have seen this organism was likely Antonie Philips van Leeuwenhoek (1632-1723) who examined his own diarrheal stool with a self-build microscope. He described that 'their bodies were a little longer than broad, and their belly was flattish and furnished with several legs'

Humans can get infected with this organism after ingesting cysts in contaminated food or water. In the small intestines, pear-shaped flagellates with two nuclei known as trophozoites replicate rapidly.
Two doctos treating a patient for worms accidentally received acetanilide instead of naphthalene from a local pharmacy. Acetanilide is broken down and metabolized in the body into this drug

Before 1982, this medication held a 37% share of the US pain relief market. However, an unknown criminal laced capsules with cyanide in Chicago in 1982 and Johnson & Johnson recalled 31 million bottles at a massive financial loss.
Approximately 25 billion doses of this over-the-counter drug are sold globally every year, yet we still don't understand the mechanism of action very well
